extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, industrial designers, patent drafters, and IP teams preparing USPTO design patent drawings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing USPTO-compliant design patent drawings, including required views, line conventions (solid vs broken), surface shading practices, and cross-view consistency checks to avoid rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven required views for complete disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy the USPTO’s requirement for a complete disclosure of the three-dimensional appearance of a design, you typically need to provide seven standard views: Perspective, Front, Rear, Left Side, Right Side, Top, Bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Missing a single angle can lead to a 'New Matter' rejection later in prosecution because you cannot add details that weren't present in the original filing. While some views may be omitted if they are mirror images or plain and unornamented (with a proper statement in the description), providing all seven is the safest path to a smooth examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings define the design claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike utility patents, a design patent’s scope is dictated almost entirely by its visual representation: 'the lines, shading, and perspectives are the claim.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the drawings are the claim, every graphical choice (lines, shading, views) can expand or limit protection. Draft with both full disclosure and strategic flexibility in mind to avoid unintentional narrowing or indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of broken lines to exclude unclaimed subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Broken lines (dashed or dotted lines) show parts of an article that are not part of the claimed design, allowing environment or non-claimed elements to be depicted without claiming them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three primary uses: (1) Unclaimed Subject Matter — show surrounding parts in broken lines (e.g., rest of phone around a novel charging port); (2) Environmental Context — indicate how the design is used (tractor attachment in solid lines, tractor in broken lines); (3) Boundary Lines — use 'phantom' lines to define boundaries where no physical edge exists. Strategic takeaway: using broken lines to exclude non-essential elements can broaden the scope of the claimed design and make 'design around' attempts harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solid vs. broken lines: strategic toggling
rubrics_metrics.description: Solid lines indicate claimed elements; broken lines indicate unclaimed elements or context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully choose which parts are in solid vs broken lines to define claim scope. Inconsistent or incorrect use can unintentionally claim or fail to claim elements. Use broken lines for background/context and phantom boundaries to avoid claiming environment or extraneous parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface shading required to show character and contour
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO requires surface shading to clearly show the character and contour of all surfaces of any three-dimensional aspect of the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper shading distinguishes concave, convex, and flat surfaces. Without proper shading the drawing may look flat and lead to 'indefinite' rejections. Ensure shading communicates contour and materiality rather than decorative texture unless that is the design feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear stippling and contour shading technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Use thin, parallel lines to indicate curvature, with lines closer together in shadowed areas and further apart in highlighted areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply consistent line direction and spacing rules across views so the same surface reads as the same contour in every view. Avoid over-dense or inconsistent stippling that obscures edges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shading conventions for transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate transparency by using light, oblique (diagonal) strokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent, light diagonal strokes for transparent materials (glass, clear plastic, liquid) so examiners can distinguish transparency from surface texture or shading for curvature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shading conventions for high-polish / mirrored finishes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specialized shading patterns to represent mirrored or metallic high-polish surfaces without cluttering the drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these specialized patterns carefully so they convey finish while preserving clarity of edges; avoid patterns that conflict with contour shading or make the figure look noisy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-shading
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective shading should provide clarity, not confusion; over-shading can obscure the design's edges and lead to 'indefinite' rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep shading balanced — enough to convey contour and materiality but not so heavy that it hides boundaries or creates ambiguity across views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent line weights across all views
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconsistent line weights (e.g., a heavy solid line in one view and a thin broken line in another) will trigger rejections for internal inconsistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure line thickness and style conventions are applied consistently so the same element reads the same in every view. Use a style guide or automated tooling to enforce consistent weights when generating multiple views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include all features consistently across views (no missing features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every feature shown in one view should appear in other views where it would be visible; missing features across views can render the disclosure incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example pitfall: top view shows a button that doesn’t appear in side profile. Perform cross-view checks to confirm every visible element is consistently represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make contours unambiguous to avoid 'vague contours' rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner cannot tell whether a surface is rounded or angled due to lack of shading or unclear lines, the design may be 'indefinite.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shading and clear edge lines to disambiguate curvature and angles. Corroborate contour cues across multiple views so the intended shape is unmistakable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform a line-by-line audit across all views
rubrics_metrics.description: A recommended quality-control step: compare each edge, vertex, and shadow across all seven views to ensure internal consistency and completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The suggested practice is a 'line-by-line' audit before filing. Every edge, vertex, and shadow must correlate perfectly across the set; this reduces 112(a)/112(b) rejections. Automated tools (e.g., AI generators) can help enforce this consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office-specific requirements and multi-jurisdictional checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Design drawing conventions vary by office (USPTO, EPO, JPO); if adapting figures for multiple filing paths, compare requirements across offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing figures for multiple jurisdictions, consult each office's drawing requirements (margins, reference numerals, paper size, shading conventions) and adjust figures or include alternative views/statements as needed to maintain compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of internal inconsistency leading to 112(a)/112(b) rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Most common rejections arise from internal inconsistency (112(a) and 112(b)), often caused by inconsistent lines, missing features, or vague contours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent these by consistent application of line/shading conventions, thorough cross-view audits, and avoiding over-shading. Use definitive statements in the description when omitting views that are mirror images or unornamented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic drafting to prevent design-arounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Use drawing techniques (broken lines, boundary phantom lines, selective shading) to broaden claim scope and make it harder for competitors to design around the claimed appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance full disclosure with deliberate exclusions via broken lines to preserve broad protection. Consider the competitive landscape when deciding which elements to show in solid vs broken lines and whether to include or omit ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of automation to enforce compliance and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated tools (e.g., AI trained on USPTO standards) can generate the seven required views with consistent line weights, compliant shading, and strategic broken/solid line toggles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automation reduces manual tracing errors and speeds drafting, but outputs should still be audited for strategic claim choices and office-specific requirements before filing.
